For Graph accounts, it needed to use graphGetMessage with the mapped Graph message ID. Fix: add a Graph branch that looks up the Graph ID and fetches via the Graph API.

The Graph branch was caching email bodies in the in-memory LRU cache but never writing .eml files to disk. When the LRU cache evicted them, they were gone. Fix: after displaying the email via the fast graphGetMessage JSON response, fire a background graphCacheMime call to download the full MIME and save the .eml to Maildir.
10.5482a7e79e4b: Failure 5: Endless spinner on email click — The initial fix for Failure 4 used graphCacheMime as the primary fetch method (download MIME, save to disk, parse, return). Fix: use graphGetMessage (fast JSON with just the HTML body) for immediate display, then graphCacheMime in the background for disk persistence. Two-phase loading: instant display, lazy persistence.
10.65897c427851: Failure 6: Thread view required collapse/expand to see content — Emails in the thread conversation view showed "Could not load email content" until manually collapsed and re-expanded. This was a React rendering race condition. The useChatBodyLoader hook stored loaded bodies in a useRef(new Map()) that started empty. The ThreadEmailItem component read from this map synchronously during render, but the useEffect that populated it ran after the first render. By the time bodies were available, the component had already rendered "Could not load." Collapsing and expanding triggered a re-render, which found the now-populated map. Fix: pre-populate the bodies map synchronously during the hook body (not inside useEffect) by checking the in-memory cache. The async useEffect still handles fetching uncached bodies, but cached ones are available immediately on first render.

For non-active accounts, it was unconditionally using IMAP to fetch headers, causing connection errors and log spam for Graph accounts. 10.ec9ee6fc2904: If you looked at our changelog today and noticed six patch releases in a single day, you might be wondering what happened. The short answer: macOS code signing and App Sandbox nearly broke us. Here's the full story.
10.b8f06d628d07: MailVault is a Tauri v2 desktop app. The frontend is React running in a native webview, and the backend is a Node.js Express server compiled into a native binary using Bun. This binary (called a "sidecar") runs alongside the main app and handles all IMAP/SMTP communication.
10.82c19b75dcb8: For macOS distribution, Apple requires apps to be signed with a Developer ID certificate and notarized. We also enable App Sandbox — Apple's security layer that restricts what the app can access on your system. It's required for the Mac App Store and is good practice for any desktop app.
10.093f67148554: v1.4.0 — Server bound to 0.0.0.0 but the frontend connected to localhost, causing IPv4/IPv6 mismatch. Fixed by binding explicitly to 127.0.0.1.
10.9790b83e5030: v1.4.1 — The "Add Account" modal used a raw fetch('/api/test-connection') instead of the API helper. In Tauri release builds, the webview origin is tauri://localhost, not http://localhost — so relative URLs resolve to the wrong place.
10.bdd7c9132592: v1.4.2 — Missing com.apple.security.network.server entitlement. The sandbox blocked the sidecar from listening on a port.
10.681ebf168715: v1.4.3 — We had shell-based process cleanup (lsof, kill) that's blocked inside App Sandbox. Replaced with Tauri's CommandChild handle.
10.899e67dc65d7: v1.4.4 — The real culprit: Bun-compiled binaries need JIT (Just-In-Time compilation). The JIT compiler allocates executable memory at runtime. While macOS has entitlements to allow this (com.apple.security.cs.allow-jit), Tauri signs all binaries in the app bundle with the same entitlements using --deep. The sidecar ended up with App Sandbox entitlements, which blocked JIT even with the allow-jit flag present.
10.e25dbeed0e20: v1.4.5 — Fixed the signing pipeline. The sidecar is now signed separately with its own entitlements (no App Sandbox, JIT allowed). The main app keeps App Sandbox. Signing order matters: sidecar first, then the main app bundle without --deep to preserve the sidecar's entitlements. Also caught that our CI pipeline was uploading Tauri's auto-generated unsigned DMG instead of our properly signed one.
10.2db4d797535c: Separate entitlements — The sidecar gets entitlements-sidecar.plist (JIT + network, no sandbox). The main app gets entitlements.plist (sandbox + JIT + network).
10.10bd74717514: Correct signing order — Sign the sidecar first with its own entitlements, then sign the main .app bundle without --deep. Using --deep would recursively re-sign everything inside the bundle, overwriting the sidecar's entitlements.
10.e8c6be521834: Look for com.apple.security.app-sandbox set to true — this confirms the app runs in a sandbox.
10.f55048f96c81: The sidecar should have com.apple.security.cs.allow-jit but should not have com.apple.security.app-sandbox.
10.bb6e68b114b3: Test release builds early. Development builds skip code signing and sandboxing entirely. The gap between "works in dev" and "works in release" can be enormous.
10.7fc3625a0333: Sidecars need special treatment. If you're bundling a Bun/Node/Deno compiled binary inside a Tauri app, it needs its own entitlements. Tauri doesn't support per-binary entitlements natively — you have to re-sign after the build.
10.0e8c41991b7c: --deep is dangerous. It's convenient but it overwrites all nested signatures with the same entitlements. If different binaries need different entitlements, sign them individually.
10.6ccece585fb7: One build script for local and CI. Having separate signing logic for local builds and CI caused the CI to upload the wrong (unsigned) DMG. Now both use the same script.

03.8a5d360574b3: The architecture behind most cloud email backup products is straightforward: the service connects directly to your mail server via API or protocol-level access, duplicates every message and attachment, and stores that archive on servers the backup provider operates and manages — not you. 03.e2a4ea47ed78: For as long as the subscription runs, the backup provider — and, by extension, anyone who successfully compromises their systems — has continuous access to your full email history. Not a snapshot from the day you signed up. An ongoing, growing archive that gets more valuable to an attacker every year it accumulates. You've traded "my provider has my mail" for "my provider and a backup vendor both have my mail," which is strictly more exposure, not less.
03.cc49908dfe40: None of this makes cloud backup vendors negligent or badly run. Reputable ones invest seriously in security. The point is structural, not a judgment about any specific company: centralizing more copies of sensitive data in more places controlled by other organizations increases the number of ways it can go wrong, no matter how well each individual party executes.
03.ab6666760867: A copy sitting on a vendor's servers can be read by that vendor's employees under the right internal access conditions, subpoenaed by a court with jurisdiction over the vendor, exposed if the vendor is breached, or handed over if the vendor is acquired by a company with different data-handling norms than the one you originally trusted. None of those outcomes require anything to go wrong on your end. They're properties of the copy existing on someone else's infrastructure at all.
03.8eb616fca188: A copy sitting on your own disk has exactly one of those risk categories: your own device security. That's a real responsibility — full-disk encryption, a locked-down machine, your own backup of the backup if you want extra redundancy — but it's a bounded, single risk you control directly, not an open-ended one you're trusting a third party to manage on your behalf indefinitely.

03.aaa1a9441508: Beyond the access question, a local copy is resilient to a specific list of failures that a cloud-to-cloud backup doesn't actually solve: the backup vendor raising prices or shutting down, the backup vendor's own service going through an outage exactly when you need to restore, a subscription lapsing because a card expired, or the vendor changing its terms of service in a direction you wouldn't have agreed to today. A file on your disk doesn't have a subscription status. It's just there.

03.0a438edc2443: The Principle Most Retention Policies Skip
03.cca258e5b93a: GDPR does not hand you a fixed retention period for email, and that ambiguity is exactly why so many organizations default to "never delete anything, just in case." But Article 5(1)(e), the storage-limitation principle, requires personal data to be kept "for no longer than is necessary" for the purposes it was collected for — and Article 5(1)(c), data minimization, sits right alongside it. Indefinite retention isn't a safe default under either principle. It's the thing they were written to prohibit.
03.bd3feaf6b3d5: In practice, this means an organization has to be able to answer, for every category of email it holds: why is this being kept, and for how much longer. "We might need it someday" is not an answer regulators accept, no matter how understandable the instinct behind it is.

03.995246466a1c: The other shift worth noting: a written retention policy sitting in a compliance folder no longer satisfies enforcement expectations on its own. 03.44066d5390a2: This is also visible in adjacent enforcement. Personal Outlook.com users got past the login screen but hit AUTHENTICATE failed when the app tried to connect via IMAP. Same symptom — "login doesn't work" — but two completely different root causes.
09.a8b013dca0af: For corporate M365 tenants, the Thunderbird app doesn't have our localhost:19876/callback redirect URI registered. Azure AD requires an exact match, and Thunderbird's app only lists Thunderbird's own redirect URIs. The fix: register MailVault's own Azure AD app with our exact redirect URI, configured as a public client (no secret, PKCE only), supporting both organizational and personal Microsoft accounts.
09.211f1b985fe4: The personal Outlook.com problem was worse. Since December 2024, Microsoft has had a server-side regression affecting IMAP OAuth2 for personal accounts. After a successful OAuth2 flow, the XOAUTH2 SASL handshake fails with "User is authenticated but not connected." This isn't a client bug — it's Microsoft's IMAP servers rejecting valid tokens. The thread on Microsoft's support forum has been open for months with no fix in sight.
09.ebab26919b51: If IMAP is broken, don't use IMAP. Microsoft Graph is a REST API that provides direct access to mailboxes without any IMAP involvement. Instead of connecting to outlook.office365.com:993 and speaking the IMAP protocol, we make HTTPS requests to graph.microsoft.com/v1.0/me/messages with a Bearer token. Same OAuth2 token, completely different transport.
09.be7201c33738: Rust backend — A new graph.rs module with a GraphClient struct implementing list_folders(), list_messages(), get_message(), delete_message(), set_read_status(), and get_mime_content(). Data structures for Graph's JSON responses (GraphMessage, GraphMailFolder, etc.) with a conversion method to translate Graph messages into our existing EmailHeader struct. Six new Tauri commands to expose it all to the frontend.
09.f444ff9468d3: OAuth2 scope branching — IMAP accounts need IMAP.AccessAsUser.All and SMTP.Send scopes. Graph accounts need Mail.ReadWrite and Mail.Send. The scope selection happens at the moment the user clicks "Sign in with Microsoft" based on whether their email domain is a known personal Microsoft domain (outlook.com, hotmail.com, live.com, and 12 regional variants).
09.d1f8250ac907: Frontend store — Every email operation in the Zustand store — loading headers, selecting an email, marking read/unread, deleting, searching, prefetching — needed an if (isGraphAccount(account)) branch. Graph messages use opaque string IDs instead of integer UIDs, so we maintain a mapping layer (_graphIdMap) that assigns synthetic sequential UIDs to Graph messages and translates back when making API calls.
09.e36c5058c890: Background pipeline — The AccountPipeline class that handles background header loading and content caching needed Graph-specific paths for both phases. Header loading uses skip-based pagination through graphListMessages instead of IMAP page fetching. Content caching downloads full MIME via graphCacheMime (a single Rust command that fetches the raw .eml, saves it to Maildir, and parses it) instead of IMAP FETCH.
